title: Acme Corp — Pricing Proposal
content: This memo records the pricing we put in front of Acme Corp during the Q2 deal cycle. After the discovery calls with their revenue operations team, we offered Acme Corp $4,200 per month for the Growth plan, with a 15% annual-commit discount if they prepay twelve months up front. The Growth plan covers up to fifty seats, unlimited call recording, and the live copilot suggestions their reps asked about. Acme's procurement lead pushed for volume pricing, but we held the monthly rate and used the annual-commit discount as the concession instead, because it protects our per-seat economics while still rewarding a longer commitment. The quote excludes the optional premium support tier, which would add a flat monthly fee on top of the plan. Billing starts on the first of the month following signature, and the discount only applies to the annual prepay path, never to month-to-month. If Acme expands past fifty seats mid-term, the overage is billed at the same effective per-seat rate. Next step is to send the redlined order form and confirm the annual-commit election before the quarter closes.

title: Globex Industries — Pricing Proposal
content: Pricing summary for the Globex Industries opportunity. Globex is a larger account than most of our mid-market deals, so we scoped the Enterprise plan rather than Growth. We quoted Globex $9,800 per month for the Enterprise plan across two hundred seats, with a 20% discount tied to a two-year commitment. The Enterprise plan bundles single sign-on, audit logging, a dedicated customer success manager, and priority failover for the streaming transcription pipeline. Globex's finance team asked for quarterly billing rather than monthly, which we agreed to at no change in rate. Unlike the Acme deal, Globex negotiated a ramp: seats phase in over the first quarter, and billing tracks activated seats until the full two hundred are live. The premium support tier is included at the Enterprise level, so there is no add-on line item. The discount is contingent on the two-year term; a one-year term would move them to the standard Enterprise rate. Our champion is the VP of Sales Operations, and the economic buyer is the CRO. We expect legal review to take about three weeks given their procurement process.

title: Initech — Pricing Proposal
content: This document captures the numbers we shared with Initech. Initech is an early-stage buyer with a small team, so we positioned the Starter plan with a path to Growth later. We offered Initech $1,500 per month for the Starter plan covering fifteen seats, billed month to month with no long-term commitment and therefore no commit discount. Initech specifically wanted flexibility to cancel, so we did not push an annual prepay. The Starter plan includes core call transcription and post-call notes but not the live in-call copilot, which is a Growth-tier feature; we flagged that upgrading to Growth would roughly double the monthly rate but unlock live suggestions. Initech asked about a free pilot, and we agreed to a fourteen-day trial capped at five seats before billing begins. There is no premium support option at the Starter level; they get standard email support. If Initech grows past fifteen seats we will revisit plan tiering. The champion is their head of sales, who is also effectively the economic buyer given the company's size.

title: Acme Corp — Hiring and Team Notes
content: Background notes on Acme Corp's team and hiring plans, gathered during discovery. Acme is scaling its go-to-market org aggressively this year. They told us they plan to hire roughly twenty new account executives over the next two quarters, which is part of why call coaching and live copilot suggestions resonated so strongly. Their current sales team is about thirty-five people, split across two regional pods, and they are standing up a dedicated sales enablement function for the first time. The VP of Sales mentioned that onboarding ramp time is their biggest pain: new reps take almost five months to reach full quota, and they believe real-time guidance during live calls could compress that. They are also hiring a revenue operations manager who would own the rollout of any new tooling. None of this touches commercial terms or pricing; it is context for the champion's motivations and for sizing future seat expansion. The hiring plan suggests Acme could grow well past their initial fifty-seat Growth footprint within a year, which is worth tracking for expansion revenue.

title: Acme Corp — Onboarding Plan
content: Draft onboarding plan for Acme Corp once the deal closes. The rollout is phased so their reps adopt the copilot without disrupting active pipeline. Week one is administrative: provision the workspace, connect single sign-on, and import the existing context documents and playbooks their reps rely on. Week two is a train-the-trainer session with the enablement lead and the two pod managers, focused on how the live suggestions surface during calls and how post-call notes flow into their CRM. Weeks three and four are a limited pilot with ten volunteer reps, chosen across both regional pods, so we can gather feedback before a full rollout. We will hold a weekly check-in with the revenue operations manager to track adoption metrics: percentage of calls with the copilot active, suggestion acceptance rate, and note completeness. Full rollout to all fifty seats targets the start of the following month. Success criteria agreed with the champion are a measurable reduction in new-rep ramp time and consistent post-call note capture. This plan is operational only and does not restate commercial terms.

title: Sales Playbook — Discovery
content: Our discovery methodology for new opportunities. The goal of discovery is to understand the prospect's current process, quantify their pain, and identify the economic buyer before any pricing conversation. Start by mapping the team: who runs calls, how many reps, and what tooling they use today. Then dig into ramp time, call quality, and note-taking discipline, because those are where the copilot creates measurable value. Use open questions and resist the urge to demo early. A strong discovery call surfaces a metric the prospect already cares about, such as ramp time to quota or win rate on discovery calls, so that later we can tie our value to a number they own. Always identify the champion and the economic buyer separately; they are frequently different people. Capture next steps explicitly and confirm them in a follow-up. Discovery is not the place to quote pricing; hold commercial terms until you have established value and confirmed budget authority. Document everything in the account record so the rest of the team has shared context.

title: Sales Playbook — Handling Objections
content: How we handle common objections. The most frequent objection is price, but price objections are usually value objections in disguise. When a prospect says we are too expensive, revisit the metric surfaced in discovery and reframe the cost against the value of faster ramp or higher win rates. The second common objection is data privacy: prospects worry about call recordings and transcripts. Our answer is that raw audio is never persisted, only transcripts, and every tenant's data is isolated. A third objection is change management, the fear that reps will not adopt a new tool; address this with the phased onboarding plan and the train-the-trainer approach. Never negotiate against yourself by volunteering a discount at the first sign of resistance. Instead, trade concessions for commitments, such as an annual prepay in exchange for a discount. If the prospect raises a competitor, acknowledge it and pivot to a differentiator rather than disparaging the alternative. Log every objection and the response that worked so the team can learn from patterns across deals.

title: Sales Playbook — Closing
content: Closing guidance for late-stage deals. By the time you reach the close, value should already be established and the economic buyer identified; closing is about removing friction, not creating urgency artificially. Send a clean order form with the agreed terms and make it easy to sign. Confirm the mutual action plan: who signs, in what order, and by when. Anticipate legal and procurement steps early, because they are the most common source of slippage at the end of a quarter. Reconfirm the start date and billing cadence so there are no surprises on the first invoice. If the deal stalls, return to the metric the champion cares about rather than pushing on price. Use commitments you have already earned, such as an annual prepay election, to keep momentum. Always summarize the agreed commercial terms in writing before signature so both sides share the same understanding. After signature, hand off cleanly to onboarding with all discovery context attached, so the customer experience stays continuous from sales into implementation.

title: Sales Playbook — Negotiation
content: Principles for commercial negotiation. Our default posture is to hold the monthly rate and use term length as the lever. When a buyer pushes for a lower price, prefer offering a commit discount tied to an annual prepay rather than cutting the monthly rate, because the monthly rate anchors renewal and expansion economics. Know your walk-away and the floor for each plan before the call. Never give a concession without getting something in return: a longer term, a case study, a reference, or a faster signature. Bundle carefully; if premium support is a real cost, keep it as a separate line so its value is visible and it can be traded. Avoid discounting the monthly rate below the point where expansion seats become unprofitable. Document the rationale for any concession so renewal teams understand why terms look the way they do. Silence is a tool: after stating a number, stop talking. Finally, keep the negotiation collaborative; the goal is a durable relationship, not winning a single transaction.

title: Internal Discount Policy
content: This is the internal policy governing discounts, for reference by the sales team. Reps may offer up to a 15% discount on Growth-plan deals without approval, provided the discount is tied to an annual prepay commitment rather than a reduction in the monthly rate. Enterprise-plan discounts up to 20% are permitted when tied to a multi-year term, again as a commit discount rather than a rate cut. Any discount beyond these thresholds requires sign-off from the head of sales, and anything that reduces the effective per-seat monthly rate below the published floor requires finance approval. Month-to-month deals carry no discount by policy, because the flexibility to cancel is itself the concession. Premium support is never discounted; it is either included at the Enterprise tier or sold as a flat add-on. Pilots and trials are capped at fourteen days and a limited seat count. The intent of this policy is to protect the monthly rate as the anchor for renewals and expansion while still rewarding longer commitments. Record the discount rationale in every closed deal so renewal teams have context.

title: Umbrella Corp — Pricing Proposal
content: Pricing summary for Umbrella Corp. Umbrella is a mid-market account that landed on the Growth plan after evaluating both Starter and Growth. We quoted Umbrella $4,800 per month for the Growth plan across sixty seats, with a 10% annual-commit discount. Umbrella wanted a slightly larger seat count than a standard Growth deal, which is why the monthly figure is higher than our typical Growth quote. They did not pursue the full 15% commit discount because they were only willing to commit to a shorter annual term with an early-out clause, so we reduced the discount accordingly. Umbrella included the premium support add-on at a flat monthly fee because their operations team wanted guaranteed response times. Billing is monthly, beginning the first of the month after signature. The champion is their director of sales enablement, and the economic buyer is the VP of Revenue. Umbrella is a good expansion candidate because their headcount is growing and the Growth plan scales cleanly past sixty seats at the same effective per-seat rate.

title: Wayne Enterprises — Pricing Proposal
content: Pricing summary for Wayne Enterprises. Wayne is a large, complex organization and was scoped for the Enterprise plan with several custom requirements. We quoted Wayne $12,500 per month for the Enterprise plan across three hundred seats, with a 20% discount tied to a three-year commitment. Wayne required a custom data residency arrangement and a security review, both of which are included at the Enterprise tier. The premium support tier and a dedicated customer success manager are bundled. Wayne negotiated a seat ramp similar to Globex, with seats phasing in over the first two quarters and billing tracking activated seats until the full three hundred are live. Their procurement process is lengthy, and legal review is expected to take over a month. The economic buyer is the Chief Information Officer, with the VP of Sales as champion. Because of the three-year term, this is one of our highest-commitment deals, and the discount reflects that. Renewal planning should note the multi-year term and the custom residency arrangement, which will need review at renewal.

title: Stark Industries — Pricing Proposal
content: Pricing summary for Stark Industries. Stark evaluated us for a single high-performing sales pod before a wider rollout, so we scoped a compact Growth deal. We quoted Stark $3,600 per month for the Growth plan across forty seats, with a 15% annual-commit discount matching our standard policy. Stark's team was primarily interested in the live copilot suggestions for their outbound reps and in post-call note automation to feed their CRM. They elected the annual prepay to capture the full discount. Premium support was declined for the initial term; they may add it at renewal if the pod rollout succeeds. Billing begins the first of the month after signature, and expansion seats beyond forty are billed at the same effective per-seat rate. The champion is the pod's sales manager, and the economic buyer is the VP of Sales, who wants to see adoption metrics from the first pod before expanding. Stark is a strong expansion candidate because a successful pilot pod would justify rolling the copilot out to the rest of their sales organization.

title: Standard Contract Terms
content: An overview of our standard contract terms, for sales reference. The default agreement is an annual term with automatic renewal unless either party gives notice before the renewal date. Payment terms are net thirty from invoice date. Billing cadence is monthly by default, though quarterly and annual prepay options are available; annual prepay is what unlocks commit discounts. The agreement includes a standard data processing addendum: raw audio is never stored, only transcripts, and each tenant's data is isolated from every other tenant. Liability is capped at the fees paid in the preceding twelve months. Either party may terminate for uncured material breach after a notice period. Seat counts are a floor commitment, and overage seats are billed at the same effective per-seat rate as the committed seats. Price increases at renewal are capped at a fixed percentage to give customers predictability. Custom terms, such as data residency or extended liability, are available at the Enterprise tier and require legal review. Reps should route any non-standard redlines to legal rather than agreeing to them directly.

title: Renewal Process
content: How renewals are managed. Renewal planning begins ninety days before the term ends. The customer success manager reviews adoption metrics, expansion opportunities, and any support issues, then prepares a renewal proposal. Our goal at renewal is to protect the monthly rate that anchors the account and to expand seat count where adoption justifies it. Commit discounts granted at the original deal are revisited: a customer renewing on an annual prepay keeps their discount, while a customer moving to month-to-month loses it, consistent with the discount policy. Price increases are capped per the contract terms to keep renewals predictable and low-friction. Watch for accounts that grew past their committed seat count during the term, because those are natural expansion conversations. Reference the original deal notes, including the rationale for any concessions, so the renewal conversation is consistent with the promises made during the sale. Flag at-risk accounts early based on low adoption metrics so the team can intervene before the renewal date. A clean renewal is one where value has been demonstrated with the metrics the champion cares about.

title: Competitive Landscape
content: A summary of the competitive landscape for positioning. Most competitors fall into two buckets: post-call analytics tools that transcribe and summarize after the fact, and generic meeting assistants that join calls as a visible bot. Our differentiators are that we run on the phone's own microphone for speakerphone calls, we provide live in-call suggestions rather than only post-call summaries, and we never join the call as a bot or use text-to-speech, which keeps the copilot silent and private. On privacy, our strongest point is that raw audio is never persisted; only transcripts are stored, and tenants are fully isolated. Against post-call analytics tools, emphasize the live copilot and faster rep ramp. Against generic meeting assistants, emphasize the mobile speakerphone capture and the absence of a bot in the meeting. Avoid disparaging competitors directly; instead, anchor on the metric the prospect cares about and show where our approach wins. Pricing is rarely the primary axis of competition; value and privacy usually matter more, so lead with those in a competitive deal.

title: Product — Growth Plan Overview
content: An overview of what the Growth plan includes, for reference during deals. The Growth plan is our mid-market tier and the most commonly sold plan. It covers up to fifty seats by default, though seat counts are negotiable, and includes unlimited call recording and transcription, post-call structured notes, and the live in-call copilot that surfaces real-time suggestions grounded in the customer's own context documents. The live copilot is the key differentiator of this tier over Starter, which has transcription and notes but not live suggestions. Growth includes standard email support; premium support with guaranteed response times is available as a flat monthly add-on. Growth deals are typically billed monthly, with an annual prepay option that unlocks a commit discount of up to 15% per policy. Overage seats beyond the committed count are billed at the same effective per-seat rate. The Growth plan is the natural upgrade path for Starter customers whose teams grow or who want live suggestions. It is also the anchor tier for expansion, since seat counts scale cleanly within it.

title: Product — Enterprise Plan Overview
content: An overview of the Enterprise plan. Enterprise is our top tier, aimed at large organizations with security, scale, and support requirements beyond what Growth offers. It includes everything in Growth plus single sign-on, audit logging, a dedicated customer success manager, priority failover for the streaming transcription pipeline, and premium support bundled at no extra line item. Enterprise supports large seat counts, commonly in the hundreds, and typically involves seat ramps where seats phase in over the first quarter. Custom requirements such as data residency and extended liability are available at this tier and require legal and security review. Enterprise deals usually carry multi-year commitments, which unlock commit discounts of up to 20% per policy, tied to term length rather than a monthly rate cut. Billing can be monthly or quarterly at no change in rate. Enterprise is where our privacy story matters most, since these buyers scrutinize data handling; the fact that raw audio is never persisted and tenants are isolated is central. Route all Enterprise custom terms through legal rather than agreeing to redlines directly.

title: Support and SLA Overview
content: An overview of support tiers and service levels. Standard support is included with every plan and is delivered over email with best-effort response times during business hours. Premium support is an add-on for Growth deals, sold as a flat monthly fee, and is bundled at the Enterprise tier; it provides guaranteed response times and priority handling of incidents. Our uptime commitment for the live transcription and copilot service is documented in the service level agreement, with credits available if we fall below the committed threshold in a billing period. The streaming pipeline is designed for failover across transcription vendors so that a single vendor outage does not interrupt a live call; Enterprise customers get priority on this failover path. Support requests are triaged by severity, with the most severe incidents, such as a full service outage, taking precedence. Customers can reach support through the in-app channel or email. Premium support customers also get a named contact for escalations. This document is operational and does not restate pricing, though it notes which tiers include which level of support.

title: Security and Privacy Overview
content: A summary of our security and privacy posture, for use in security reviews. The foundational principle is that raw call audio is never persisted; audio is processed in real time for transcription and then discarded, and only the resulting transcripts are stored. Every tenant's data is isolated from every other tenant through row-level security in the database, and this isolation is adversarially tested so that one customer can never read or write another customer's data. API keys for the underlying vendors are held by the company and never exposed to client devices. The copilot is silent by design: it never joins a call as a bot and never uses text-to-speech, so the other party is unaware of it. Data in transit is encrypted, and access to production systems is restricted and logged. Enterprise customers can request custom data residency arrangements, which require review. Deletion is honored on request, with soft deletion followed by purge routines. This overview is often the deciding factor in competitive deals where the prospect is concerned about call data, and it pairs with the contract's data processing addendum.
